explanations.explanation: That's the one. God tells Moses, Israel's leader, “…as God Almighty, but by My name the LORD I did not make Myself known to them.” (Exodus 6:3) So Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Israel's forefathers, knew Him as God Almighty. Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and I can tell you hearing your own name again is a gift.

God Most High sounds mighty and holy, and I see why it tempts you. But in Exodus 6:3 God says He appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty. That's the name He gives there. He also says He did not make Himself known to them by His name the LORD.

The Everlasting God is a lovely name, friend. But it isn't the one in this verse. God tells Moses He appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty, and that He did not make Himself known to them by His name the LORD (Exodus 6:3).

Yes, foreigners. God calls Canaan “…the land where they lived as foreigners.” (Exodus 6:4) Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Israel's forefathers, lived in the very land God promised to give them. I think that makes the promise feel even bigger.

Rulers sounds grand, baker, like somebody handed them a crown. But God calls Canaan “…the land where they lived as foreigners.” (Exodus 6:4) That's how the verse describes Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in that land. God also says He made His covenant with them to give them the land. I think that makes the promise even sweeter.

It's a good guess, but this verse isn't about their jobs. God says Canaan was the land where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived as foreigners (Exodus 6:4). That's how the verse describes their stay there. Priests don't come into it.

Right, groaning. God says, “Furthermore, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving…” (Exodus 6:5) He also says He has remembered His covenant. I think it's a comfort that He names the very sound they were making, friend.
I wish it were singing, baker. But the Israelites are being enslaved by the Egyptians, and God says He has heard their groaning (Exodus 6:5). That's a hard sound, and it's the one He names.

A feast sounds nice, friend, but this verse has no table in it. The Egyptians are enslaving the Israelites, and God says He has heard their groaning (Exodus 6:5). That's the sound He names. Feasting isn't in the verse.

explanations.answer: With an outstretched arm and mighty acts of judgment
explanations.explanation: That's it. God says, “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment.” (Exodus 6:6) Notice who is doing the work. It's God saying "I will," not the Israelites pulling themselves up. Friend, I can't even reach the top shelf without my mustache.

explanations.answer: With a ransom of silver and gold paid to Egypt
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a business deal, but it isn't what God says. In Exodus 6:6 He says He will redeem them with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment. No payment to Egypt is mentioned in the verse. God does the acting Himself.

explanations.answer: With a covenant of peace and gifts for Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: Gifts for Pharaoh, king of Egypt? Not in this message. God says He will redeem them with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment (Exodus 6:6). He is the one doing the rescuing, and the verse doesn't mention any gift basket.

explanations.answer: Take them as His own people
explanations.explanation: Yes! God says, “I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God.” (Exodus 6:7) The leaving is only part of it. He is also taking them as His own. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so being wanted means a lot to me.
The verse never says that, baker. God says He will take the Israelites as His own people and be their God (Exodus 6:7). Being His people is the promise. Nothing here is about ruling Egypt.

Haran isn't in this message. God says He will take them as His own people and be their God (Exodus 6:7). Then He says He will bring them into the land He swore to give Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 6:8).

True. God says, “And I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession.” (Exodus 6:8) He swore it to the forefathers, and now He says it to their children's children. That's a promise with a long memory.

This one is true, friend. In Exodus 6:8 God says, “I will give it to you as a possession.” He is talking about the land He swore to give Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Good thing the verse ends with “I am the LORD.”, so we know who is promising.

I can see why you'd hope so after a message like that. But the text says, “…they did not listen to him.” (Exodus 6:9) So the answer is false. They didn't listen to Moses, even with all those promises.

False is right. Moses relayed the message, but “…they did not listen to him.” (Exodus 6:9) Good news was on the table, and it didn't land. I think that tells us something about how heavy their load was.

explanations.answer: Their broken spirit and cruel bondage
explanations.explanation: Exactly. The verse says it was “…on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage…” that they did not listen (Exodus 6:9). I think when you're that worn down, even good news is hard to hear. This is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Their love for the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say they loved Egypt. It says it was because of their broken spirit and cruel bondage that they did not listen to Moses (Exodus 6:9). Cruel bondage is not something a person loves. It's something that wears a person down.

explanations.answer: Their trust in the gods of Egypt
explanations.explanation: This verse doesn't mention any gods of Egypt. It gives the reason plainly: “…on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage, they did not listen to him.” (Exodus 6:9) So it's about how crushed they were, not who they trusted.

explanations.answer: If Israel won't listen why would Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: That's his reasoning. Moses says, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me…” (Exodus 6:12) He's looking at how his own people reacted and doing the math. I bet it felt like a very fair question to him.

explanations.answer: Pharaoh is far too powerful to face
explanations.explanation: That's not what Moses says. His reasoning is, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me…” (Exodus 6:12) He points to his own people not listening. He never says anything about Pharaoh's power.

explanations.answer: The Israelites are not ready to leave
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that here, friend. He says, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, then why would Pharaoh listen to me…” (Exodus 6:12) His point is about being listened to. It isn't about whether Israel is ready to leave.

Yes, speech. Moses says he is “…unskilled in speech?” (Exodus 6:12) I think he's nervous about talking to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Friend, I'd be nervous too, because my best speech so far is mumbling through a mustache.

Battle is a good guess, baker, but it isn't what Moses says. He tells the LORD, “…I am unskilled in speech?” (Exodus 6:12) Speech is the word he uses about himself. I think he's thinking about Pharaoh, king of Egypt, since that's who the LORD sent him to.
Writing isn't what Moses says, baker. He says he is “…unskilled in speech?” (Exodus 6:12) I think his concern is about standing up and talking to Pharaoh. That's talking, not writing.

explanations.answer: Everything the LORD says to him
explanations.explanation: Right, everything. God says, “I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I say to you.” (Exodus 6:29) There's no trimming and no leaving out the hard parts. Moses is a messenger, and the whole message goes.

Close to the idea of Aaron helping, baker, but not who picks the words. God tells Moses to pass on everything He says to him (Exodus 6:29). Then God says Moses speaks all that He commands, and Aaron is the one who tells Pharaoh to let the Israelites go (Exodus 7:2). So Moses carries the message and Aaron is his prophet, his spokesman. Aaron doesn't get to edit the script.

The verse doesn't narrow it down like that. God says, “tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I say to you.” (Exodus 6:29) Everything is a whole lot more than one warning. The word "plagues" isn't in that verse.

Yes, prophet. God tells Moses, “…your brother Aaron will be your prophet.” (Exodus 7:1) Aaron, Moses' brother, is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go out of his land (Exodus 7:2). Moses had said he was unskilled in speech, and I think a brother at his side must have been welcome news.

A bodyguard is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the job. God says, “…your brother Aaron will be your prophet.” (Exodus 7:1) Aaron's part is speaking, since he is to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go (Exodus 7:2). Guarding isn't in the verse.

Writing things down isn't the role God gives Aaron. The LORD says, “…your brother Aaron will be your prophet.” (Exodus 7:1) A couple of verses later, Aaron is the one to tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites go (Exodus 7:2). That's speaking, not scribbling.

That's what He says. God tells Moses, “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and though I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt…” (Exodus 7:3) The text doesn't give a reason here, so we don't add one. It's a heavy line, and we let it stand as written.
I wish it went that way, friend, but it's the opposite. God says, “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart…” (Exodus 7:3) The text doesn't say He will soften it. Hardened is the word.

Search is a fun guess, friend, but it isn't the word. God says, “But I will harden Pharaoh’s heart…” (Exodus 7:3) Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, and the verse says harden, not search. That's the word God uses, so we leave it right there.

I get why you'd think so, baker. More signs and wonders sounds like it should change a king's mind. But God tells Moses that Pharaoh will not listen, even as the signs and wonders multiply (Exodus 7:3-4). So the answer is false. God goes on to say, “Then I will lay My hand on Egypt…” (Exodus 7:4)

False is right. Even with His signs and wonders multiplying, God says, “Pharaoh will not listen to you.” (Exodus 7:3-4) Then He says, “…by mighty acts of judgment I will bring the divisions of My people the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 7:4) So Pharaoh not listening is part of what God tells Moses, and He still says what He will do.

Yes, the Egyptians. God says, “And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them.” (Exodus 7:5) So it's not only Israel who will know. The people in Egypt will know it too.

The Canaanites aren't named in this verse. God says the Egyptians will know that He is the LORD when He stretches out His hand against Egypt and brings the Israelites out (Exodus 7:5). The Israelites are leaving Egypt, so the Egyptians are the ones watching.
The Philistines never come up in this passage, friend. God says, “And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD…” (Exodus 7:5) The verse is about what happens in Egypt. The Egyptians are the answer.

True. “So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them.” (Exodus 7:6) Moses had said twice that he was unskilled in speech (Exodus 6:12, 6:30). I bet that wasn't easy, but they did just as He said. Friend, that's an ending I'd frame.

It's true, baker. The text says, “So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them.” (Exodus 7:6) Moses had said he was unskilled in speech, and I bet he felt nervous. They still did it. I know a thing or two about doing something when you're nervous.

Eighty. “Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.” (Exodus 7:7) That's Moses' age at the moment the two of them speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Aaron, his brother, is eighty-three. That's a lot of years behind two men walking in to speak to a king.
Not forty, baker, he's a lot further along than that. Exodus 7:7 says, “Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.” So Moses is eighty.
Sixty is close in spirit but not in number. Exodus 7:7 says Moses was eighty years old when they spoke to Pharaoh. Aaron was eighty-three. Both of them had plenty of years behind them.

Yes, eighty-three. The text says, “Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.” (Exodus 7:7) So Aaron, Moses' brother, is three years older than Moses. Three years apart, and the two of them walk in to speak to Pharaoh together.
That's too low, friend. Exodus 7:7 says Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh. Moses was eighty. Aaron is the older of the two.
That's a big jump. Exodus 7:7 says Aaron was eighty-three, and Moses was eighty, when they spoke to Pharaoh. Ninety-nine is too high by sixteen years.
